actions.text: Good morning, everyone! I’m Ella, and I’m thrilled to welcome you to our web‑development adventure.
First, let’s look at what this course is all about. Our main goal is to help you build a simple web page using HTML, even if you’ve never written a line of code before.
We’ll start with the basics: document structure, headings, links, images, lists, tables, forms, and why semantic HTML matters.
The format is short, progressive lessons with quick quizzes and a hands‑on activity at the end, so you’ll get plenty of practice right away.
That’s the roadmap for today—let’s jump in and start building something amazing together!

actions.text: Alright, let’s dive into HTML Basics and the structure of a web page.
First, HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language – it’s the backbone that gives web pages their structure and meaning.

Here’s a simple diagram showing the hierarchy: the document starts with <!DOCTYPE html>, then the <html> tag wraps everything, inside we have <head> for meta‑info and the <title>, and finally the <body> where all visible content lives.
Remember, every tag is written with angle brackets, like <tag>. Don’t worry if that feels new – you’ll get the hang of it quickly.
That’s the core skeleton of any HTML page. Any questions before we move on to building our first page together?

actions.text: Now let's check what we've learned about the basic HTML skeleton. You'll see two questions—one about the correct tag order for a minimal page, and another about the element that holds the page title.

For a minimal HTML5 document you need three things in this exact order: the <!DOCTYPE html> declaration, the <html> root element, and inside it a <head> section followed by a <body>. The <title> tag belongs in the <head>. Option A follows that structure perfectly, while the other choices either miss the doctype, place the <head> after the <body>, or omit required tags.

The page title is defined with the <title> tag, and it must appear once inside the <head>. Its text shows up in the browser’s title bar or tab, but it never appears inside the page content itself. So statements A, B, and D are correct; the title element should not be repeated, making statement C false.

actions.text: Alright, everyone, let's dive into adding links and images to our web pages. These two elements make a site interactive and visually engaging.
First, the basic hyperlink syntax: we use the tag with an href attribute. It looks like link text. Replace "url" with the destination address and "link text" with what you want users to click.
Here's a concrete example that opens a new tab: Visit Example. The target="_blank" part tells the browser to open the link in a separate tab.
Notice the quotation marks around the URL and link text—always keep them paired, otherwise the browser gets confused.
Now, to embed an image, we use the tag with a src attribute, like . The alt attribute provides a text description for accessibility.

elements.content:
• Use <a href="url">link text</a> to create hyperlinks

• Use <img src="path" alt="description"> to embed images

• Remember to set target="_blank" for external links

<a href="https://example.com" target="_blank">Visit Example</a>
<img src="image.jpg" alt="Sample Image" width="200">
